newsitem.title: JAPAN: DKB cuts bosses' pay, deposits fall again.
newsitem.headline: DKB cuts bosses' pay, deposits fall again.

text.p: Scandal-tainted Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd said on Tuesday it had cut the salaries of its 32 board members and five auditors by five percent to 60 percent.

A bank spokesman said president Katsuyuki Sugita had his pay cut by the largest amount -- 60 percent -- followed by 45 percent each for two vice presidents, to take responsibility for being involved in illegal payoffs to a racketeer.
The pay cuts began in July, and the spokesman said it has not been decided yet how long the cuts will be in place.
Separately, a DKB spokeswoman said there were again heavy withdrawals of deposits last month as individual customers pulled about 199 billion yen from their accounts.

The spokeswoman said the drop in individual deposits in July followed a decline of nearly 150 billion yen in May. Deposits rose in June due to payments of half-yearly bonuses to Japanese workers, but the increase was a comparatively small 7.0 billion yen.
Individual deposits totalled 13.1 trillion yen at the end of July.
Analysts said the slide in deposits reflected a drop in the bank's credibility because of the racketeer payoff scandal, but added that the decline was unlikely to seriously hurt the bank's earnings.

"The decline in the deposits is a reflection of the negative image caused by the scandal, but I don't think it will have any major impact on DKB's performance," said Yoshinobu Yamada, a financial analyst at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc. "The bank's assets total more than 50 trillion yen."
On July 30, the Ministry of Finance (MOF) announced administrative penalties against DKB and Nomura Securities Co Ltd for their involvement in the scandal.
Under the penalties, DKB was ordered to stop making loans to new clients, except for key housing loans, from August 6 to December 31.

It was also banned from selling mutual funds, called investment trusts in Japan, at its branches, or making use of financial holding companies or liquidating assets by new methods for a year from August 6.

Analysts said, however, that the penalties were unlikely to have any serious impact on DKB's performance, as there is little demand now for loans, and the financial deregulation process to allow the sale of mutual funds at banks and to establish holding companies remains unclear.
The DKB spokeswoman said the bank was working out a programme to strengthen its internal supervision as ordered by the ministry.
